summary: This experimental document describes how ForCES can model a network device's packet parallelization datapath, using constructs from the ForCES model and controlling it with the ForCES protocol.

eli5.summary: Some devices process many packets at the same time. This RFC shows how to describe and control that side-by-side work.

questions: how does forces model parallel packet processing
what is flood vs split parallelization
how do splitter and merger lfbs work
when should you use packet parallelization
subtitle: Processing multiple packet streams at once in network forwarding elements.

tldr.problem: Modern network devices can process packets in parallel, but the ForCES model had no way to describe or control this parallelization.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7409 adds three new Logical Function Blocks (LFBs) to ForCES: a Splitter that divides a packet for parallel processing, parallel processors, and a Merger that reassembles the results.
tldr.outcome: Network administrators can model and manage parallel packet processing pipelines, improving performance in high-speed devices.

today: RFC 7409 is an Experimental specification. It extends the ForCES model to support parallelization and has not been updated or obsoleted.

sections.title: Parallel Packet Processing in Network Devices
sections.content:
ForCES (Forwarding and Control Element Separation) is a framework for describing how network devices forward packets. The ForCES model uses Logical Function Blocks (LFBs)—modular processing stages connected in a pipeline. RFC 7409 extends this model to handle packet parallelization: situations where a device processes multiple streams or packet fragments at the same time.

This RFC introduces three new LFBs for parallel processing: a Splitter that starts parallel work, intermediate processors that run on parallel paths, and a Merger that collects and reassembles results. The design is inspired by Cilk, a parallel programming language, using its concepts of "spawn" (start parallel work) and "sync" (wait for and collect parallel results).
sections.eli5: A packet is like an order at a restaurant. Normally it goes through steps one at a time. Parallel processing means different parts of the order can be prepared at the same time—one chef fries fries while another grills burgers.

sections.title: Two Types of Parallelization
sections.content:
RFC 7409 defines two parallelization methods: Flood and Split.

In Flood, a single packet is copied and sent to multiple processing paths in parallel. For example, a packet might be sent to both a classifier (to determine its type) and a metering engine (to measure its rate) at the same time. Implementation can use either physical copies or logical pointers, depending on the device's design.

In Split, a packet is divided into equal-sized chunks, and each chunk goes to a parallel processor. For instance, packet bytes could be hashed in parallel or pattern-matched across multiple regex engines. Like Flood, the split can be physical (truly dividing data) or logical (sending pointers), and distribution to processors is implementation-dependent.
sections.eli5: Flood is like saying a message to multiple people at once. Split is like tearing a page into pieces and giving each piece to someone to read.

sections.title: The Splitter and Merger LFBs
sections.content:
The Splitter LFB marks the start of a parallel region. It takes a single input packet or flow and creates parallel tasks: either copies of the packet (Flood type) or packet chunks (Split type). Each task carries a Task Correlator—a 32-bit identifier that tracks which parallel task comes from the same original packet.

Processing LFBs in the parallel paths operate independently. The Merger LFB waits for all parallel tasks with the same correlator to arrive, then reassembles them into a single output packet. The RFC does not specify how Merger handles ordering or timing—that is left to implementation.

Nested parallel regions (a parallel path containing another Splitter-Merger pair) are not allowed in this version; designers must use only a single level of parallelization per datapath.
sections.eli5: The Splitter says "process these parts at the same time" and labels them so they remember they belong together. The Merger collects them all back and glues them into one piece again.

sections.title: CoreParallelization LFB and Control
sections.content:
To enable control over parallelization, RFC 7409 introduces a CoreParallelization LFB. This special LFB does not process packets; instead, it advertises the device's parallelization capabilities. A Control Element (CE) queries this LFB via ForCES protocol to discover which LFBs can be parallelized, with which other LFBs they can be paired, and in what order they can be assembled.

The CoreParallelization LFB is part of the FEObject (Forwarding Element). Through it, the CE can discover and configure the parallelization options available on that device, adapting the datapath topology to the device's hardware capabilities.
sections.eli5: CoreParallelization is like a device telling its controller "I can split and merge packets, and here are the tricks I support." The controller uses that info to set up the right parallel paths.

sections.title: LFB Library and Standards Considerations
sections.content:
RFC 7409 includes XML definitions for the three parallelization LFBs in the ForCES LFB Class Library. Because this is an Experimental specification, the LFB Class IDs are in a range above 65535 (reserved for experimental use), and the LFB names begin with the prefix 'Ext-' (Ext-Splitter, Ext-Merger, Ext-CoreParallelization).

This RFC does not mandate physical implementation details: whether copies are true memory copies or logical pointers, how chunks are distributed to processors, or what happens if merger tasks arrive out of order. These choices are left to the device implementer. The focus is on the control plane model—how the CE describes and commands parallel processing.
sections.eli5: This is an experiment, so the names and IDs are marked as temporary. Different devices can implement the actual parallel processing differently as long as they speak the same language.
